speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-175, to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act (equal residence requirements accorded alien spouses of Canadians).

speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SAME RESIDENCE REQUIREMENT FOR ALIEN HUSBAND AS FOR ALIEN WIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the present time an alien wife of a Canadian citizen may be granted citizenship when she has resided in Canada for only one year, but an alien husband of a Canadian wife must have resided for five years.
The purpose of this bill, therefore, is to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act to provide that there is no difference between the residence requirements for the acquisition of Canadian citizenship by an alien husband and an alien wife of a Canadian citizen.

speechtext:
Order, please. The House again in committee of the whole on Bill C-170, to amend the statute law relating to income tax. When the committee rose on Monday, April 9, clause 19 of the bill was under discussion. The hon. member for Bellechasse was seeking to be recognized. He is now recognized if he wishes to be.
On Clause 19-Depreciable and other Capital Property of Deceased Taxpayer.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned I was making a few remarks on Bill C-170 and since then, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) tabled an announcement that he will amend certain clauses. Since these amendments generally seem to satisfy the requests which have been made, I will wait until we are studying certain clauses of the bill to make representations.
As for clause 1, I would have preferred more significant advantages to be granted to the individual as regards basic exemptions. I admit that some improvements have been made to the bill but, in my opinion, they are not sufficient and do not match those requested.
Those were the few remarks I wanted to make at this stage; I will again raise certain subjects when the bill is studied clause by clause.

speechtext: Shall clause 19 carry?

Clause agreed to.
On clause 20-Election by Legal Representation and Transferee Re Reserves.

Mr. Chairman, there is no difficulty with this clause, although I am wondering about the intrusion of a different principle by this clause. Frankly, I think it should have been included in clause 19. We are considering clause 20, subclause (1), and this ought to have been included as clause 19, subclause whatever. This matter does not affect the Income Tax Act although, so far as clause 20 is concerned, there is no difficulty with it whatsoever.
I should like to ask the minister, when he answers in speaking on clause 20, subclause (1), to deal with something that should have been clarified in clause 19. When we are considering depreciable property and there is the transfer by devolution to the child from the deceased taxpayer, I take it this provision covers all the buildings and improvements to the property of a depreciable nature, save and except the principal residence which is covered by Section 40 of the act. There has been some uncertainty about this. Perhaps the minister could clarify precisely what is going to be covered in this exemption
Income Tax Act
from capital gains, first at the time of death and, second, the inter vivos transfer under the amendments that the minister has introduced. Presumably the same assets are going to be covered.
I will also want a full explanation as to the value of the capital asset which shows up in section 73(3), paragraphs
(e), (i) and (ii). This appears in the left hand column of page 3 in Votes and Proceedings under the notice given by the minister where the valuation is deemed to be the capital cost of the transferor, not that of the transferee. I think we will get into a little bit of difficulty there.

Mr. Chairman, I can give the undertaking to the hon. member and the committee that both on the transfer by death and the transfer inter vivos, during the lifetime, pursuant to the amendment I tabled, the free transmission involves all depreciable property, including buildings and equipment, original or improved. As the hon. member has suggested, the principal residence is already taken care of under another provision.
The hon. member's reference to paragraph (e) of section 73(3) is a relieving provision. This simply provides for the continuity of the cost provisions in respect of the depreciable property. I think that I can assure the hon. member that this again is a relieving provision.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question. It involves the transfer of the property of a farm family at death under the projected amendment. Is depreciable farm machinery included in this provision? In what manner will it be replaced or how will this be done? I think this is a very important area because of the high capital cost of farm machinery. I am particularly aware of the high capital cost of farm machinery for western grain growers. I would also like to ask the minister to clarify the distinction between the straight-line depreciation turnover and what I think is called the depreciated balance.
Diminishing balance.

Diminishing balance. The loss of this straight-line depreciation has been very keenly felt. I have received many more representations on this than on the capital gains tax on the family farm. I would like to see the straight-line depreciation carried on when the asset is passed from the parent to the son or daughter. I urge the minister to reinstate this straight-line depreciation. I believe that more than anything else, it has provided for a very strong economic base in agriculture. I think it is very important that this straight-line depreciation be carried on and expanded at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, these provisions, of course, apply primarily to the diminishing balance standard of depreciation and include that balance as applied to a depreciable property, as I defined earlier for the hon. member for Edmonton West. With regard to the straight-line depreciation, this is covered in Section 13 of the act. It is unaffected by these provisions; not narrowed, not widened.

Whatever is left can be carried forward by the new owner.
I believe that is the case, Mr. Chairman. We will give the hon. member further confirmation of that. If there is anything different to report, I will let the hon. member know.

Mr. Chairman, we have covered two cases. There is one point. It was my understanding the minister was also providing for the rollover. However, I now take it that would not now be included. I am referring to the rollover where the farmer, inter vivos, sells farm A in order to acquire farm B. There is no provision for that.

Mr. Chairman, there is no provision for that. The rollover provisions only apply to depreciables of a prescribed class under the capital cost allowance system, since the farmer can already sell straight-line depreciables with a straight-line capital gain. We do not see a problem there.

Although I know the minister does not want to deal with incorporated family farms, under this legislation he is not providing for the situation where a farmer is going to sell his present farm, which may be too small, or for some other reason, and will immediately acquire a farm down the road. He may be moving from an orchard property to a corn growing property. There would still be the problem of capital gains with respect to this farm land transaction.
That is so, Mr. Chairman, because it is not a continuation of the same farm. It is a barter, exchange or sale and purchase of a new farm property.

Mr. Chairman, when we were completing the business the other night, I asked the minister a question. I do not believe he has answered it. I wonder whether he would do so at this time. It was with regard to the evaluation that is being established on farm properties. At the present time, I do not think there is any provision whereby a farmer can confirm with the Department of National Revenue or the taxation department that his property has been evaluated and that the evaluation will be acceptable in future years and to future governments.

Mr. Chairman, there is quite a division of responsibilities in the administration and interpretation of the taxation policy. From time to time the Minister of Finance, whoever he or she may be, has the responsibility for tax policy, brings it forward to the House and committee and interprets it in terms of its own intentions. As hon. members know, those words are not binding on a court of law. The court, the Tax Review Board or the Federal Court will look at the statute as they find it. My words today or the words of any minister are not relevant in the interpretation of the statute. The parliamentary intention must be sought by the words of the statute itself, not only with regard to the tax law, but the Criminal Code or any other statute.
There is also a distinction in responsibility between the tax policy, which at the moment is mine, and the adminis-
tration of the act, which is the responsibility of my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue. There is nothing in this bill or the amendment I introduced Thursday evening that bears on the problem raised by the hon. member. There is nothing in this bill, nothing in the amendments I introduced Thursday night, which bears on the question raised by the hon. member. I do not have the authority to respond to his question, except to say once again that I will draw the matter to the attention of my colleague and impress on him the importance the hon. member attaches to it.

Thank you. This is an important question. Valuation has to be established upon some basis, and if it is left in the hands of future generations the government will, no doubt, find itself in a position of unfair advantage. It is an issue which the government will be obliged to clear up, either through the Department of Finance or the taxation branch of the Department of National Revenue.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with the amendment having to do with capital gains. Will he tell us his definition of a child? Is it the same as the definition here, which reads:
"Child" of a taxpayer includes a child of his child and a child of his child's child.
That is the extended meaning of "child" applicable to this transfer provision. Is the same definition used in the amendment the minister is bringing in? Will it include the grandchild?

I do not want to begin discussing the famous law against perpetuities which the hon. member for Edmonton West and I could argue, or the cases in British law involving what we used to call fertile octogenarians. The bill says:
For the purposes of subsection (9), "child" of a taxpayer includes a child of his child and a child of his child's child.
In other words, it includes children or grandchildren.
Or great grandchildren.

Or great grandchildren. If, by reason of accident or predecease, there was a gap in the generations the benefit could go on to a further generation as long as the farm stayed within the family by direct descent.

Are farm partnerships, at the present time, or under the amendments, treated in the same way as farm corporations? There are a great many farm partnerships in existence throughout Canada, situations in which fathers and sons, or two or three brothers, are operating under partnership agreements. Would the minister clear up this matter?
The rules apply only to individually held farms, since it is the family farm we are trying to preserve. They do not apply to partnerships or corporations.

That being the case, is the government prepared to consider a further extension of this principle,

because there are a great many important implications here for the farming community?

We are certainly prepared to look very sympathetically at the partnership question. The farm corporations pose far greater difficulty for us because they also involve non-farming small business as well. But I can go further into that, if the hon. member wishes.

Secretary of State for External Affairs and seconded by the President of the Privy Council by way of amendment.
Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt these amendments?

The only comment I wish to make is this. I am very sorry the government failed to look into the question of the incorporation of the family farm. It is my information, and I take it as being reliable, that as of today there are about 8,000 family farm corporations in the country. Relative to the number of farmers in Canada the figure may seem small, but I put it to the minister that these 8,000 farms could readily account for between 30 and 40 per cent of agricultural production in this country. They are the heart and core of the bigger producers, particularly in the prairie provinces, though I am sure that if the minister would travel through southwestern Ontario he would find that the tobacco
farmers, the dairy farmers and, certainly, the beef growers, are almost to a man incorporated.
This has been the thin end of the wedge. I am glad to see the principle has been recognized. It vindicates an amendment I put forward at the time the Finance Committee was making its report to the Minister of Finance. The government has at last recognized the principle that the family farm should, at this stage at least, be exempted from capital gains tax. I trust we shall see an extension so that the whole range is dealt with. Certainly, speaking on behalf of my colleagues, I commend this position as being one we would take.

A brief comment, Mr. Chairman. We, of course, support the amendment introduced by the minister and congratulate him on introducing it. I should like to say also he was very wise to accept the view of my party in this regard. I believe it was progressive move. We all recall that an amendment to the same effect was moved last year by a former member of this House, Mr. John Burton. It is an important step in keeping alive the family farm not only on the Prairies but throughout the country.

I have taken note of the comments made by the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken. I just want to say that the caucus of the party to which I belong was also instrumental in bringing about this decision. I want to give particular credit to the hon. member for Bruce.

The minister tells us his caucus was instrumental in getting the government to change its mind. Members of my party and members of the party to my left have tried for more than three years to bring some sanity to this legislation as far as the family farm is concerned. All I can say is that if a new caucus on the government side has been able to help bring about changes in this important field, let us have another election very soon so that we can benefit from either a new government or a new caucus, in order that still further changes may be made. It has been a "tax to form" bill, in view of what the Minister of National Revenue said. If these tax conformities are not clarified so there is a further conversion of Paul on the road to Damascus, as the Minister of Finance mentioned today, then they will be by other governments in the not too distant future, so that the Canadian public has a tax law that is not only equitable but sane and sensible, and can be understood by them.

Mr. Chairman, essentially this section permits a taxpayer to defer the recognition of income for tax purposes until such time as his investment has been recovered. It relates to section 80(1) which is the section providing for rules for determining the income of a taxpayer who has had a business carried on abroad which was expropriated by a foreign government.

Mr. Chairman, this, then, in essence, is to prevent from being taken into income at one time, or over two years, the total value of a foreign asset that has been expropriated; the resident Canadian taxpayer is therefore allowed to prorate it. He can also elect to take the income, if there are any securities of the acquiring country or authority, and accumulate that income so it becomes capital to the total value of the capital at the time of the expropriation. Thereafter it is treated as income but subject to income tax; is that so?
Basically, that is it.

Mr. Chairman, this is an amendment to the French version of paragraph 81(l)(c) and removes the word "ou" from the phrase "d'un navire ou d'un aeronef ou qu'elle exploite dans un trafic international". Clause 23(2) is a relieving amendment which exempts from taxation various forms of income accruing from property awarded to a person under 21 years of age in respect of personal injury. An example of persons who would benefit from this provision are the victims of the drug thalidomide.

Mr. Chairman, about 15 months ago we made an amendment reducing legal age to 18 so as to conform with what is now considered to be the age of an adult, and since in most provinces today the legal age of an adult is 18, why are we reverting to the age of 21 rather than going down to the plateau of 18, as I think we should?

Mr. Chairman, to look at this from another point of view, we are trying to exempt income building up on a compensation award, leaving it free of tax until the person is 21. So, it is really for the benefit of the child that the income be allowed to accumulate from an award until he is 21, rather than 18. This provision has nothing to do with majority, minority or civil responsibility; it is purely a relieving measure.

Mr. Chairman, last Thursday night I brought some comments to the attention of the Minister of

Finance regarding the section of the act that is being amended by this clause of the bill. If I may refresh the memory of the Minister of Finance, it had to do with disability payments paid under supernannuation or retirement plans. Before I go any further, I wonder whether I could ask the Minister of Finance if he remembers the points I made?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman put it in such articulate terms, there is no way I could forget. He raised a question about the taxation of workmen's compensation payments made to injured firemen employed by the borough of Scarborough. I am advised that workmen's compensation payments made to injured firemen employed by the borough are being exempted from tax. Workmen's compensation is a provincial responsibility, but it is my understanding that as a Schedule II employer, 75 per cent of the normal wage paid as workmen's compensation is not being subjected to income tax. The additional 25 per cent amount paid by the employer is being subjected to tax.
In the case of permanent disability, it is my understanding that a similar exemption is being accorded to amounts payable as workman's compensation. Since the administration of the act is involved here, perhaps if the hon. member has any specific case he would refer the situation to my colleague the Minister of National Revenue.

May I thank the Minister of Finance for his compliment about my articulateness, but in spite of my reputation I guess my point was still not made; I am sorry about that. I was not referring to firemen working for the borough of Scarborough; it happened to be firemen who had been working in the past for the Toronto fire department. I understand that Scarborough and Toronto are very close neighbours, so I can see where the minister made the mistake.
I was not talking about people who are receiving benefits from the workmen's compensation board, be it in the province of Ontario or any other province. I understand that they are quite clearly covered by the provisions of the present act in section 81(l)(h). I was talking about people who in the past had received disability payments at a time when their working unit was not covered by workmen's compensation by reason of provincial law. The case I employed as a clear example of this was that of the Toronto fire department.
The Toronto fire department had a very ancient and venerable superannuation, retirement and disability plan of its own, and it was not until the late 1950's that the Toronto firefighters were brought under the workmen's compensation board. Before that time, if the firemen were injured they received disability payments, not from the workmen's compensation board but out of their own superannuation and retirement funds. But these payments were clearly disability pensions.
Since the late 1950s-staying with the example of the Toronto firefighters-firemen who are injured and who receive disability payments from the workmen's compensation board do not have their pensions taxed. The unfortunate persons who worked for the fire department before it came under the workmen's compensation board do have their disability pensions taxed.

The point I was trying to make to the minister was this. Would he consider making an amendment to bring the pensions of these people within the terms of the act having to do with income that is not to be included in any amount that is calculated to be taxable? That is quite a different matter from the one to which the minister just referred.
As I said the other night, Mr. Chairman, there is no reason in simple justice why these people should have their disability pensions taxed. The cases I have in mind are those of people who have appealed to the income tax department and have been told time and time again that nothing can be done because of the law, although their cases are just and will be reported to the Department of National Revenue. Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the opportunity to make a few comments about partnership rules on the basis of a discussion I had with my own accountant and an article written by Donald R. Huggett which appeared in the Canadian Chartered Accountant. He suggested that in attempting to find a reserve for 1971 receivables it is the individual partners of a partnership who will have the real problem, not because of any particular equity or anomaly but because reserve limitations are so difficult to grasp and computations are virtually impossible to make with any degree of accuracy. He said:
As stated, individual partners must bring into income in 1972 their share of 1971 receivables which were not previously taxed, but they are permitted to deduct a reserve therefrom which, in the case of expanding firms, may result in the postponement of tax until retirement or later years. It is the computation of the "reserve" that will give many professionals fits-
He goes on to state that the actual cost is not so difficult to calculate, and then states:
Fair market value of a partner's interest may be a difficult figure to determine and no rules are prescribed (naturally) for its computation. However, it may be significant to note that the proper figure is the fair market value of the partner's interest and not his share of the fair market value of the partnership.
I think this is of some importance in assessing tax equity. Mr. Huggett also states:
Unlike the computations for cost and fair market value, the calculation of tax equity must be made at the partnership level. Once established, it must then be apportioned among the partners. No rules are provided for the division of tax equity among partners and one can only assume that the number of methods will approximate the number of professional partnerships in Canada. Unfortunately, playing the tax game without rules is almost as dangerous as playing Russian . . . roulette-
He then went on to say in the final paragraph:
While the various provisions seem logical, there is no doubt that they are extremely complicated and that it would be extravagant for each and every partner of a professional firm to spend the time required to attempt to comprehend them in full.
I think this is an area in which partnerships have a very shady and dim path to follow.

Mr. Chairman, clause 34 is one of the clauses which has made it urgent that this bill be passed.
It should have been through in December.

Yes, or two or three years before that. The desirability of getting the clause through, of course, is so that refunds may be made which a number of pensioners have claimed on filing their returns, refunds which we understand have been computed and are ready to be mailed. What this clause does is to raise to $1,000 the extra exemption a taxpayer can claim if he is 65 years or over. For the year 1971, that figure stood at $500. It was raised by a previous piece of legislation to $650 for the year 1972. However, if this clause goes through, that $650 will never have been in effect and instead the figure will be $1,000 as from January 1, 1972.
I suppose there are few pieces of legislation before this parliament that will receive such quick and ready endor-sation, but because it is so popular and so certain to be passed I dare to ask a question about it, even at the risk of appearing to question motherhood. If my memory is correct, and I think it is, the first time when an extra exemption for old age was added to the basic income tax exemption was at a time when the government was being pressed to increase the amount of the old age pension. It did not feel it could do so and thus this concession was made. It was my own thought at that time that this was a temporary arrangement and that when the time came for pensions to be made universal, and of a more substantial amount, that the extra exemption which originally was $500 at age 70 I believe, or was it to start at age 65-I think it started at age 65.
It was suspended in 1964.

Then, for a while it was suspended for those receiving old age security between the age 65 and 70. At any rate, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister whether this time around any consideration was given to the alternative, namely, that instead of a charge on the treasury of this kind, that is allowing this extra exemption, that the amount of money involved might be used to raise the actual amount of the old age pension. My point is that when you allow this $1,000 exemption it is fine for all those who have income taxes to pay, but what about the million-I think that must be the number-persons over age 65 who do not pay any income tax at all? This extra $1,000 does not mean a cent to them. To those who pay a little income tax this $1,000 exemption may mean a bit, or if you go at it in another way those in the upper brackets receive a fairly high percentage reduction and those in the lower brackets receive a lower amount.

Is the minister familiar-I am sure he must be-with the history of this? Has some consideration been given along the way to using this money to increase the actual amount of the pension? I submit that $15 or $20 added to the actual pension of everyone would be more of benefit to the persons on old age security than this benefit. There are some organizations, notably organizations of women in this country, which have made quite a study of this matter and have recommended this very course. I do not know whether the recommendations have reached the minister, but I hope they have. Even though it may sound a little academic to ask a question about this matter which will be passed very quickly, I should like to ask the minister whether thought has been given to the alternative that instead of the extra exemption, which means nothing at all to one million old age pensioners, the amount involved here could have been added as an additional amount to the old age security pension itself.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I would have to review the various philosophical thrusts behind the three types of old age pension. The first is a universal pension paid across the board, regardless of need and means to everyone in this country 65 years of age or over. That is in consideration I believe of the productive efforts and initiative that our older people have put into the country, as a reimbursement to them for that effort and also as a means of supplementing their income after their earning days are over. Added to that on a basis of need is the guaranteed income supplement for those whose resources are insufficient. The raising of the exemption, on the other hand, from $500, then to $650 and now to $1,000 is in recognition of those people of moderate means-more than moderate means sometimes-and people of less than moderate means who during their lifetime have sacrificed in order to provide some kind of capital assets from which they derive income. This is as an encouragement to them to set something aside and as a recognition of the fact that such incentive is worthwhile in our society.
If they were to build up a property of $10,000, $20,000, or $30,000, or now in the case of working men and women, capital far in excess of that, then the income they draw from it might be $3,000, $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 a year in addition to what they have by way of old age pension. I suppose the philosophy is that the exemption should be raised for those people as an extra incentive. For single persons aged 65 or over there would be a basic exemption of $1,500, the optional standard deduction of $100, and the special deduction for age proposed in the bill of $1,000, making $2,600. No income tax is paid by persons over 65 up to $2,600. For married persons there is the $1,500 exemption plus the additional exemption for married persons of $1,350, again the optional standard deduction of $100, and the proposed special deduction for senior citizens of $1,000. So, for someone over 65 who is married, the total exemption is now $3,900 and no tax is paid on that amount.
The purpose of this amendment is to encourage the setting aside of a nest egg, of savings, to encourage the

curtailment of consumption for future use. Perhaps that is a worthwhile motive in our society.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to add anything to what was already said on second reading and to all the protests I have made about the pressures now being put by the government to get this bill through now because time is operating to the prejudice of senior citizens, but primarily-and some are becoming most excited about this-to the students who are on the other end of the scale. The polity should be made by the government to the taxpayers concerned because these were provisions that were brought in in the budget of May last year and the bill introduced in June of last year. Here we are in mid-April, and these people are still not able to obtain their refunds.
However, the point that I want to make is directed more to the Minister of National Revenue than to the Minister of Finance. As you know, there is form TD1 wherein the taxpayer is the subject who files with his employer, or the person paying him the income he makes, indicating the extent of the exemptions that he is claiming. We have provisions for people of married status and we have a provision for wholly dependant persons, and we also have provisions for persons over 65, but it was drawn to my attention yesterday afternoon over the telephone by a person who is directly affected that there is no provision for the claiming of an exemption by a disabled person who is entitled to the $1,000 exemption. As a matter of fact, the person in question is an employee of the government of Canada, and that person is not able to file a TD 1 form and obtain a $1,000 exemption but must claim it at the end of the year through a refund. In this particular instance the refund to that person has been held up. If that person has a statutory right to an exemption, why should the TD 1 form not provide for it?
I do not think this is the same sort of thing as one can claim a little later on under section 35 for attendants allowance for a totally disabled person. In this particular case I make a strong recommendation that the Minister of National Revenue take a look at form TD 1, and let us reverse the process for these disabled persons.

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated when I was speaking a few minutes ago, I do not wish to delay the passing of this clause or even the passing of this bill, but I would like to say that I appreciate the answer which the Minister of Finance gave in response to my comments. He indicated that there are different groups of people and that the purpose of this provision is to recognize the position and the rights of those who have some savings of their own. That is a point of view that I share, especially when we come to the question of universality. It is precisely for that reason that I do not think there should be any means test on old age pensions at all. But that is an argument we can make on another occasion.
The point I would like to make-and I hope the minister will accept it-is that in spite of all the fanfare there is about this, at least one million old age pensioners get no advantage out of this at all. The number of old age pensioners who qualify for the guaranteed income supplement, according to the latest figures I have, is about 58 per

cent of the total, or 58 per cent of 1,800,000, which is about 1,045,000. Of course, people who qualify for the guaranteed income supplement are getting money that itself is not taxable, so with these new limits they are not taxable in any case.

In other words, even with the higher rates of pension and the higher rates of guaranteed income supplement, the number of Canadians over 65 who qualify for at least a portion of the guaranteed income supplement is rising. Mr. Chairman, on second reading of this bill I presented an idea to the minister regarding the expenses incurred for medical purposes when the individual has to travel from his residence to some other spot where the facilities are available. At that time I was not looking at the bill but at the statement the minister made about it on May 8, 1972. Clause 35(3)(viii.l) at the bottom of page 57 of the bill provides that those expenses can be deducted if a number of things happen, one of which is if payment is made:
to a person engaged in the business of providing transportation services, to the extent that the payment was made for the transportation of
In this instance, the taxpayer has to make the payment to a person engaged in providing transportation services; in other words, he has to hire a transportation vehicle when he is 25 miles or more away from the facility. From my own experience travelling around th^ country, I know that there are a number of places where commercial transportation is not available in any convenient form. In a northern area it is not unusual for people living close to the communities to own their own boats, yet have no medical facilities available in the community. In others, people are disadvantaged by the lack of commercial transportation and have to use automobiles while in the far north it is a question of aircraft. People who own their own aircraft may have to use them to travel for medical attention.
I think the construction of that subparagraph which says that the demand must be made "to a person engaged in the business of providing transportation services" would deny the opportunity for the deduction in cases where there were no commercial transportation facilities to take the patient 25 miles or more for medical attention. I suggest that this subparagraph should be amended. I drafted the amendment and sent a copy to the minister so that he could consult with the people who are in the business of drafting. I do not know whether my suggestion is acceptable, but I think we should remove subparagraph (viii.l) entirely and substitute the following:
to a person engaged in the business of providing transportation services-
Which is how it reads at the moment, and add the words:
or for transportation by a mode of transport owned by the taxpayer at rates not in excess of those provided by regulation for any such mode of transport to the extent that the payment was made for the transportation of
The additional words are, "transportation by a mode of transport owned by the taxpayer at rates not in excess of

those provided by regulation". The difficulty I had in trying to adopt language that might be acceptable, in order that an acceptable and reasonable figure might be arrived at, was compounded by the fact that, as mentioned earlier, it is difficult to know how much a mode of transport may cost. For instance, in coastal areas people normally travel by boat, usually their own boat. I do not know how much it costs per mile to run a boat. Cost varies with the size of the boat, and I do not know what a reasonable cost would be. Similarly, varying figures could be used in connection with the operation of a motor vehicle. We are allowed 16 cents per mile, and in other areas the allowance is 14 cents, and so on. It is difficult to spell out these amounts. Again, in the far north or remote areas of the country people own their own aircraft. I do not know how much it costs to travel by aircraft. What the reasonable figure would be I do not know.
I thought that this matter might best be decided by regulation which might spell out what is a reasonable cost for the various kinds of transportation that a person might use. To stretch the point, in the depths of winter, in the northern most points, the mode of transportation would be dog sled, I presume. I do not know what are the cost factors involved in that mode. As it may be necessary to spell out these costs in great detail, that matter might better be left to regulation. I hope the words of the amendment cover the point I am trying to make. If my suggestion is acceptable, I think it may ease what otherwise would be a discriminatory application of this particular concept.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time I have heard a Minister of Finance stand up in committee and say this is a good idea, but we will have to let National Revenue look at it. I sometimes wonder whether anyone from National Revenue in a responsible decision making capacity ever moves out of this capital. Perhaps the people who live in the communities the hon. member for Skeena was talking about are not as wily as some urban dwellers. I do not know. Why would a thing like this be difficult? It is a matter of geography; more than 25 miles. If that is not enough to satisfy the hon. member for Edmonton West, let us make it 27 or 28 miles. It is a simple matter of geography. There are maps of Canada that show how far it is from point A to point B. Surely, somewhere within the apparatus of the government of Canada there are facts available with regard to where medical facilities are located. If the Department of National Revenue does not have that information, surely it could be supplied by Statistics Canada or the Department of National Health and Welfare.
With regard to the question of evasion, this could be covered by the submission of some kind of voucher supporting the claimed deduction. If it has to be validated by an appropriate medical authority stating that the person was in fact required to travel from his place of residence to a medical facility in order that the claim could be scrutinized by the Department of National Revenue, that would not be a very difficult requirement. I appreciate the

Income Tax Act
minister's remark that he wants to make sure this is administratively feasible. However, I certainly hope what is essentially a sound proposal to achieve fairness will not be sidetracked, as is so often the case. There is a recent example of this in an information bulletin which was issued the other day; it dealt with the question of expenses at remote sites.
We in this chamber must recognize the realities of life in the various parts of Canada. We should try to make the law fair to those people who accept the advice the Prime Minister has been handing out rather freely in recent months to go to the places where the work is and produce the wealth. Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss some of the clauses on page 59 which deal with allowances for students and ask for some reconsideration so that greater help can be given to students, parents and others from many of our middle class families. The incomes of many of these families are too high for them to receive much of the government aid that is available through grants and loans and, at the same time, are so low they find that financing education for their young people is not easy.
I congratulate the minister on the proposals appearing on page 59. They indicate a great deal of progress in this
(Mr. Barnett.]
area, first in recognizing the principle that the cost of university and other education should be deductible and, second, making some very admirable provisions for it. Good as the provision is, I think it ought to go much farther. I hope the minister will give consideration to the comments I will make and to the suggestions I will offer.
I first wish to point out that this proposal only allows for one variable, that is the variable of the student's income. According to this proposal, he may deduct $50 a month times the number of months he is enrolled in the institution. In the case of the sponsoring individual making the income tax return, he may deduct the student's taxable income. A much more important and relevant variable for the student or his family is the way the fees vary. According to the proposals on page 59, considerable advantage is given to a person attending a certain kind of educational institution, such as a community college where the fee may only be in the neighbourhood of $250 a year. A student attending for nine or 10 months of the year can claim a deduction of $450 or more. Compare that with the need of the student who is enrolled in a scientific course that may involve him paying a fee in the neighbourhood of $1,000. He can only claim the same deduction as the person paying a fee in the neighbourhood of $250. Some consideration should be given to providing for this variability in the kind of fees our students and their families are paying.
I suggest it could be covered if the bill were changed so that the student or his sponsor might deduct $50 multiplied by the number of months of the year during which the institution is attended, or the tuition fee, whichever was the greater. This would be of considerable help to students enrolled in expensive courses. These students do not all come from high income families. Many are attending these institutions only through great efforts by themselves or by their families. They do not make up a great number of taxpayers, and I think we would find that the value of the help to them would far exceed the burden it might place on the government.
I should like to comment, now, on another subject. Clause 35 makes provision for students attending universities outside Canada, but as far as I can see not for students attending other post-secondary institutions which do not offer degrees. I find it difficult to understand why non-degree-granting institutions within Canada should be on the list of designated institutions while those outside Canada are not. I think we should take into account the needs of students attending nursing schools, art schools and other educational, institutions, which, if they were in Canada, would be on the list of designated institutions.
It sometimes happens that students need to go outside Canada to attend courses which are not available here, and I do not think they should be penalized for doing so. Further, I would point out that we offer the opportunity to a Canadian taxpayer to deduct where a student is enrolled in a non-degree-granting institution outside Canada if the student commutes to such an institution, but not if he is a full-time resident. Again, it is hard to see why this distinction should be made. A student living within driving distance of the United States border might,
April 12, 1973

for example, be able to attend an engineering school, or a school of technology, or a nursing school, there, and benefit from this concession. On the other hand, if he lived hundreds of miles from the border and was obliged to live near the school of his choice, he could not claim this reduction.
Finally, I would ask that the minister give considerable thought to the possibility of permitting an allowance for parents who send their children to privately-funded schools. According to the most recent figures I have, there are 147,628 boys and girls attending schools of this kind. Many of these children will not go on to universities or colleges. They do not come from high income families. Most of them are in these schools because of profound religious and moral convictions on the part of their parents. The families concerned support the public sector of the educational system through taxation, though they do not necessarily benefit from it. They have to meet, from their own resources, often at great sacrifice, the cost of educating their children at these private schools. I myself am profoundly committed to the concept of the public education system, but I believe we should have equal respect for those who are looking after these private institutions. I suggest that opportunity be given for the parents of such children to deduct all or part of the cost of private education from their taxable income. This would go a long way to assist Canadian parents who because of religious and moral convictions find themselves bearing a very heavy burden.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to consider the question of income from educational trusts. I am informed that such income is subject to taxation even though the money derived from the funds will be going to the children. I have received complaints that parents have to regard such income as taxable and I hope the minister will consider exempting income derived from educational trusts from definition as taxable income.
The minister has done something which will receive support from all parts of the House and of the country in recognizing the principle which characterizes his proposals, but I trust he will give serious thought to improving these provisions so as to help a large number of families and individuals who are making an honest effort to advance themselves.

A few comments having to do with allowances in respect of students attending certain types of educational institutions. I have received a number of letters from the Edmonton area where parents of nurses have gone to the Department of National Revenue for a ruling as to whether or not student nurses qualify under the section we are considering. They were given a negative answer. They did not qualify because nurses were not attending a degree-granting university. I should like to point out to the minister that those who decide to become members of the honourable profession of nursing work very hard for five or six days a week without pay for what they do. It is true they may receive some benefit by way of board, but the responsibility for their maintenance is a responsibility of the parents. These students will graduate from nursing schools supported by the departments of education in their respective provinces. These nursing schools are entitled, under provincial laws, to grant
Income Tax Act
degrees. Why, in these circumstances, are nurses not accorded the benefits of this section? I shall have more to say on this subject in a few moments after I have heard the minister's response.

I wish to make a few comments on the subject dealt with by the hon. member for Scarborough East. He may think every member of every party agrees with him, or with the general principle enunciated in this clause having to do with clause 35(6)(h). Speaking as a Member of Parliament and as a taxpayer-and as a taxpayer who benefits from this section-I am less than enthused about this proposal. I have not worked out a detailed calculation, but I have a daughter who attends university for seven months of the year. Based on a total of $350 for the year, in my particular tax bracket I suppose I would save somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100 to $125 a year. I admit that I do not mind getting that saving, but once again it seems to me that we have a relatively new provision in our income tax law that benefits people in the top income brackets of this country who least need the help.
I do not have the actual figures in front of me, but if I say that 80 per cent or more of the young people who attend universities-not community colleges but universities-in Canada come from the upper or middle income groups, I am certain that I am making a relatively conservative estimate. Yet it is precisely this group of people, the young students or their parents, who will benefit from this provision that was brought in last year, I think it was. This is one more illustration of how over the years we have brought into our income tax law special provisions that have eroded the progressive nature of the income tax law and given advantage to people in the upper and middle income brackets. We all know that, particularly since the end of world war II, the gross national income in Canada has risen each year somewhere between 5 and 9 per cent. We know that most people in Canada are living better than ever before, and we all like to think that in recent years we have been moving toward a more egalitarian and equitable society. But that is not the case.
Some questions that I asked both last year and this year and which were answered by Statistics Canada demonstrate conclusively that those in the upper income brackets in this country are each year getting a larger percentage of the gross national product, whereas the people in the lower income brackets are getting a progressively smaller percentage of the gross national product. The question I asked last year and this year was a simple one. I asked what percentage of the total money income was received by the lowest fifth, the second lowest fifth, and so on, of the people in Canada in terms of family units.
What did I find in the answer I was given both last year and this year? I found that in 1957 the lowest 40 per cent of the Canadian people received 16.1 per cent of the total income earned in Canada. In 1967, this percentage dropped to 15.6 per cent, and in 1971, the last year for which there were figures, it went down even more, dropping to 14.2 per cent. On the other hand, the upper 40 per cent of the income earners of this country experienced a reversal of this trend. In 1957, they received 65.9 per cent

April 12, 1973
Income Tax Act
of the income, in 1967 they received 66.6 per cent, and in 1971 the percentage was 68.2 per cent.
Some people will say: "Oh, but that is before taxes. Our tax system, transfer payments, pension payments and welfare payments work the other way, and people in the lower income brackets receive a higher percentage of the total income and resources of this country". I do not believe that is true. My belief, which I must admit was an intuitive belief, was reinforced by a study released in December 1972 by the Economic Council of Canada entitled "The Pattern of Taxation in Canada". The author of the study was Allan Maslove, and he deals precisely with what taxes the various income groups in this country pay.
For the sake of brevity, Mr. Chairman, I shall paraphrase the question he asks and the answers that are given. His answers are fully documented in great detail, with a whole series of statistical charts that I would commend to the Minister of Finance and the members of this House. One of the questions Mr. Maslove asked was: Who pays for the various governmental activities; and who, in the final analysis, actually pays-bears the burden of-the tax? Mr. Maslove says that virtually all taxes have the potential to affect the relative economic positions of an individual family in two ways: by affecting the income received-the income-sources side; or by altering the relative prices of the goods bought-the income-uses side. The net effect of these two adjustments, according to Mr. Maslove, is to change the real income position of the individual as compared to his pre-tax position and relative to other members of the community.
Mr. Maslove then analyses taxes on the basis of whether they are progressive; in other words, whether they increase in percentage and in amount as incomes rise, or whether people in the lower income brackets pay more of their income in taxes. He says that the extremely regressive nature of the tax system at the low end of the income scale and the lack of progressivity over the remainder is quite apparent. He points out that from 22 to 39 per cent of the people, depending on province, in all family units are in the lower income range, having an income of $6,000 or less per year.
Mr. Maslove then asks who pays for government programs. He says all of us who pay taxes pay, and most of us do. He then asks which group bears proportionately the heavier burden of taxation, and his answer is that it is the lower income families. Who bears the least of the load proportionately? It is those with higher incomes, particularly those with incomes over $12,000 a year. I suggest that the bulk of students attending Canadian universities come from families with incomes over $12,000 a year. I make no secret of the fact-indeed, even if I wanted to I could not- that I am in this category. Yet it is precisely people like me who get the tax break. Someone in the 50 per cent tax brackets who has one child going to university for seven months of the year will save $175 a year, and I suppose that I shall save about $125 a year. Any person making $6,000 a year whose child attends a university-there are some, but fewer than the hon. member for Scarborough East seemed to suggest-will have only a minimal tax reduction.
While I am not going to oppose this, I would tell the minister-

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion before us there are some preliminary remarks I wish to make relating to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. When the present government was first elected in 1968, I was not a member of this House. However, it was my impression that the government espoused two priorities: first, linguistic equality of both of Canada's official languages and, second, removing some of the regional economic disparities that exist in Canada.
May I say that I endorse the underlying principles put forward. I also endorse in general terms the objective of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is that industrial incentives be made available in particular regions following their designation by the federal government after consultation with provincial governments. Surely, many aspects of economic development must be considered when one talks about industrial expansion. One could mention transportation and geographic isolation. Our transportation system must span these geographically isolated communities as much as possible.
One must also look at DREE programs from the point of view of the capitalization necessary for small and medium size industries. There is great potential in so-called designated areas, but if this potential is to be utilized and realized there must be outside help with capitalization. As the hon. member who just resumed his seat suggested, it is necessary for there to be co-operation between federal, provincial and municipal governments and with private entrepreneurs if this potential is to be realized.
If I may speak directly to the motion, the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) wishes specific documents to be produced. I agree that to some extent certain aspects of DREE activity should be made public and come under scrutiny. The activity mentioned in the motion, however, is not an area that should be made public because a certain amount of confidentiality is necessary in connection with the loan application and those who review it. If private entrepreneurs are to avail themselves of government help, specifically that given by DREE, they must be confident that their financial position and other internal matters pertaining to the company do not become the property of the public.
I shall now speak specifically about the convention centre, or the Commonwealth Holiday Inn mentioned in notice of motion No. 76. As I come from Manitoba, may I point out a few factors of which the hon. member may not be aware. As hon. members know, Winnipeg, by virtue of its location in the mid-continent, is uniquely placed for the development of convention and tourist facilities. It is
April 12, 1973

fairly closely related to large metropolitan areas of the United States such as Minneapolis, Minnesota. It is quite accessible from the mid-western United States.
The province of Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg, specifically Unicity, have been able to get together, the result being that private entrepreneurs are now developing what is known as a convention centre in Winnipeg. That centre will contain recreational facilities and will be suitable for the holding of large and small conventions. The Commonwealth Holiday Inn is part of this complex and of the development of the inner city of Winnipeg. I am speaking as a Manitoban who lives 40 miles outside Winnipeg. This centre will be an asset not only to Winnipeg but to all Manitoba. That is the type of development we are looking for from DREE.
The hon. member suggested that the money spent should have been made available to small businesses. I agree. However, a guaranteed loan of this nature does not rule out any loans that might be made to small or medium sized businesses. So I endorse what has taken place with the assistance of local and provincial officials in Manitoba whose work has enabled us to include this Holiday Inn as part of our convention facilities.
In anticipation of the completion of the convention centre we have already seen in the general area of Winnipeg the development of hotel facilities which are second to none in North America. Mr. Speaker, if you relate the hotel facilities and the number of rooms we will have in Winnipeg to the population of Manitoba, you will see why we anticipate economic development as an ancillary effect of the convention centre through the expanded tourist industry.
Almost all of Winnipeg is regarded as a designated area under the DREE umbrella. I refer to the city itself. I have been speaking more of rural areas and their development. I could say that Winnipeg should not be included as a designated area, but I cannot be so provincial. Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal have gained a reputation, in many circles, and if you are holding a convention it is thought it should be in one of those centres. We in Manitoba, specifically Winnipeg, are trying to prove that this is not the case. Winnipeg has facilities which make it a viable convention area.
As an aside, I might say that Commonwealth Holiday Inns have built a facility in Kenora, Ontario, which is just outside my constituency. speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at five o'clock it was considering clause 35.

Mr. Chairman, when I was discussing this subject earlier today I was making the point that while I have no particular objection to this clause which gives tax benefit to a taxpayer who has a dependant attending university, I feel it is just one more example of benefits being given to people in the middle and upper income brackets. I draw attention to the figures made available by Mr. Maslove in the study he carried out for the Economic Council, which showed conclusively that people in the lower income bracket pay a substantially higher percentage of their income in taxation to the three levels of government than do other taxpayers.
Since I spoke earlier this afternoon I have learned that the government of Ontario has announced it will increase sales tax from 5 per cent to 7 per cent.
Shame.

I suppose there are very few taxes more regressive than sales tax. The only example I can think of are municipal taxes which are paid on property without any relation to wealth or income. Other than this, there is no tax more regressive than sales tax. All the studies show that people in the lower income bracket pay substantially

more this way as a percentage of their income than do taxpayers in other income groups.
We have made some progress. It is not often I commend the minister, but I commend him now on the very progressive step he took when reducing income tax rates. I commend him for weighting the benefits of these cuts instead of providing a flat rate which would, again, mainly benefit those in the middle and upper income brackets. I have been reading a book entitled "The Rape of the Taxpayer," written by a former senior civil servant in the United States treasury department, Mr. Philip Stern. He gives an illustration of what I have in mind. He points out that if Governor Nelson Rockefeller, for example, were to make a donation of $100,000 to one of his favourite charities, the Museum of Modern Art in New York city, his liability for income tax would be reduced by $70,000. So in effect he would be given $30,000. But if a schoolteacher gave a donation of $10 to the museum, the tax deduction would amount to only two or three dollars.
This is the kind of inequity we have incorporated into our income tax laws over the years by means of special clauses and subsclauses designed to help somebody or other, usually those in the middle and upper income brackets. Consequent upon the income tax reduction which I am sure will be approved by the House-I am thinking specifically of the 5 per cent reduction-every taxpayer will get an immediate reduction of $100. But for many people in the lower income bracket, particularly married men with dependants, the reduction of $100 is, in fact, not 5 per cent but as much as 45 per cent. That is the kind of tax policy thinking that I should like to see the minister not only continue but expand.
May I close by giving the minister an illustration of what I mean by referring to something that was done this year in the province of Manitoba. The Manitoba government put through a program called the education property tax credit plan. They took the view that every person who owns his own house or rents accommodation for himself and his family is paying, in his municipal taxes, for the support of the educational system in his area. The government have taken the view that the burden of local taxes is becoming too onerous; therefore they have devised a tax credit plan under which every person who pays income tax is entitled to a credit of a minimum of $50 and a maximum this year of $147. Next year the maximum will go up to $200.
The difference between that plan and most other tax plans that I know about is that the minimum $50 is given to people in the middle and upper income brackets, whereas the maximum of $147 this year and $200 next year benefits those in the lower income bracket. As one's income increases, so one's tax credit decreases. Not only does it give a tax credit to those who pay income tax; it gives a rebate to people whose income is so low that they are not required to pay income tax. The province is encouraging these people to fill out an income tax form, and has opened offices with staff to help people who are not accustomed to paying income tax to fill out the form and mail it to the provincial finance minister. In return they get a cheque in the form of a rebate under the plan. The Minister of Finance is beginning to think along those
April 12, 1973

lines. I think he has made a good beginning, though he has not gone nearly far enough in his income tax reduction this year.
My last point is this. I trigd to make it clear in my remarks before the dinner hour that I did not object to this particular form of tax aid to people with dependants at university. However, it is time we looked at our whole income tax structure in this country and revised the system, wiping out most, if not all, of the concessions given to special interest groups, whether they be in the oil or mining industry or any other industry. We should do what the Carter commission said, which essentially was that we should regard a buck as a buck and people should pay taxes on that basis.

May I draw to the attention of the hon. member for Scarborough East section 60, subsections (e), (f) and (g) of the existing act where he will see tuition fees generally are deductible. This is an educational deduction generally for the student, for his spouse or his sponsor. I think when they are read together it will be seen that we have broadened this deduction a good deal.
The hon. member then spoke of non-degree institutions, particularly outside of Canada. I suppose this is a policy decision that will have to be reconsidered at some time, but the impetus has been to try to persuade our students to get their education in this country. He then referred to the commuter problem. We will take another look at that, but at the moment we find there is not enough policy thrust for his suggestion.
In respect of secondary institutions the hon. member is getting into the separate school question. The federal government has stayed constitutionally clear of primary and secondary education. We are involved in post-secondary education, educational manpower training for employment, and recycling. I think I would have great difficulty persuading the provinces that this was not an initiative already in their domain, and I am afraid I cannot recommend to this House that we get into it. The hon. gentleman should direct his question to the Ontario government.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister referred to nursing associations, did he mean a nursing association, or individual nurses? In the province of Alberta, for example, would they be certified, or could each individual nurse be certified?

Any nursing association anywhere in the country, if it could persuade the Department of Manpower and Immigration to recognize the

April 12, 1973
Income Tax Act
profession of nursing, or a particular school of nursing, as a qualified institution within the regulations would be eligible and that would be the end of it. I would suggest that the Alberta nurses ought to see what they can do to get the various training schools in the hospitals qualified within the regulations of the Department of Manpower and Immigration; they would then be qualified within the section and the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few comments on what the minister has said. First of all, under the provisions of the existing legislation, as I understand them, a student is entitled to deduct tuition fees, but I do not recall a sponsoring individual having that right.
That is right.

My plea was on behalf of the sponsoring individual having an equal right to that of the student. With deference to the minister's remarks, I should think further changes would have to be made to the legislation before us; or perhaps the minister will bring in something new to give the sponsoring person the same right the student apparently now has.
Secondly, in respect of what the minister said about secondary education, I do not think this gets us into the separate school issue per se, because it involves many other institutions. The reason the province of Ontario has not seen fit to pay the costs of students from grade 11 on is that from grade 11 these institutions are regarded as private schools.
Therefore, I was referring to all secondary institutions privately funded, which includes institutions sponsored by many religious groups, Christian, Jewish, Protestant, Evangelical, and other persuasions some of which have no religious reference at all. Parents send their children to these schools because of their own convictions. It seems to me when parents are sponsoring the public educational system through taxation, but because of their own particular convictions have a desire for another form of education for their children, they should have this advantage. In this instance I feel the federal government should agree.
Rather than looking at this matter in the parochial way, I think it is back in the lap of the Minister of Finance. I hope at a subsequent time he will bring forward a measure to give these people as much relief as possible. I think the minister should do this as an example of what might be done in the future. The government has accepted the principle that the cost of education can be deducted not only for students but for sponsoring individuals, and I think we will see steady progress in this area over the years with the government providing more and more assistance year by year. This is very often a technique used by government. It is very much like the salami technique, under which you offer a slice this year, a little more next year, and so on. I think we can look for progress. However, I wish the minister would not be so content to wait, but would give the people, now, what they really need.

Mr. Chairman, I want to pursue the point again with the minister about people who are disabled. Would he have his officials look at this clause once again?

It seems to me a bit unfair the way it stands. I am not trying to make a political point here, but a number of people who are genuinely disabled or invalid are not necessarily confined to a wheelchair or to bed.
It seems to me this legislation could contain a clause that would provide for eligibility under a doctor's certificate or statement to the effect a person is unable to work or pursue his occupation. That should be enough to qualify him for the $1,000 exemption on the spouse's income. Would the minister consider standing this clause for the evening and having another look at it to see whether he could possibly include this type of provision to make the legislation more equitable for people who are disabled? Many people in this country have disabilities but do not receive adequate pensions or assistance, either federally or provincially, and a provision such as this would be a small help to them in remedying the situation.

We are being quite specific here, Mr. Chairman, in that we are referring to individuals confined to bed or a wheelchair. This is the essential purpose of the relief, and we prefer at this time to leave it at that. We will take the hon. member's problem under advisement, but we are specific in the parameter of relief that we are covering.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether his department has a definition of blindness, because this is very difficult to define. Does he have guidelines he could send to the people who are affected?
Mr. Chairman, there is nothing within the statute to define blindness. This, again, involves a question of fact. I suppose it could be by medical certificate.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to be asking more questions on this matter but I am still not clear as to what is required. The minister says nurses know what to do, but it strikes me as rather peculiar that they have not done it. He went on to say they have to persuade the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to allow them registration within the department. Perhaps he could clarify with regard to the apparent stumbling-block in the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It seems to me that a school which is qualified or recognized for training nurses should automatically qualify.

Obviously, the need has not arisen. But if the hon. member would look at page 61 of the bill and the amendment to section 110 of the Income Tax Act, specifically the definition of an educational institution on the third line of page 61, he would see that an educational institution in Canada is a university, a college or other educational institution. Then if he looks down to paragraph (B) he will see that it covers being certified by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration as an educational institution by which courses are conducted that provide or improve the qualifications of a person for employment or for the carrying on of a business or profession.
Since nursing is a profession, all that needs to be done is to have the particular institution qualify within these regulations. That is my advice to the hon. gentleman. The particular association of nurses or the hospital he has in
April 12, 1973

mind just need to apply; and if they meet those general criteria, I cannot see any problem.

Mr. Chairman, would it not be much more simple if the minister spoke to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and asked him to automatically certify all nursing schools which offer degrees in nursing-that would simplify the matter-rather than having each individual association appear before the manpower group. Would it not be much more simple to automatically recognize them if they offer degrees?

I am not so sure of that. I think it would cause more problems than it would solve. We have general criteria which apply, for the purposes of the Canada Student Loans Act, to education, tuition fees and other aspects of education. There are the same general criteria for all programs. There has been a lot of experience with this program and it seems to have worked pretty well so far.

Well, for any type of school, perhaps; but they must meet the standards of the act. I think we found in practice in the past that setting general criteria and having the facts established within them is the better way to deal with it. Every time we specifically add one institution, we thereby exclude every other institution. It is better to have a general set of criteria which apply equally to business schools, recycling schools, manpower training, and so on. I do not think the case will meet much difficulty in being met.
