Income Tax Act
We have now dealt with the increased exemptions for people over age 65 and we have dealt with increased allowances for students. I have found it rather interesting in the last few days to note that somehow or other certain categories of taxpayers all of a sudden are in a great rush. Up to a week or ten days ago there was great silence, particularly from students, about the inability to obtain refunds. This matter was raised in the House. I raised it in a speech, as did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). Then there was a statement by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) about the number of files or returns that were banked, shall we say, and that authorization from the House was being awaited in order to pay out the refund cheques or process the files. Some, certainly, may be ready for pay-out; in others, the matter of assessment may be involved.
However, I thought it was not quite in keeping with the realities of the situation when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the other day stood up and solemnly requested from the House early, almost peremptory passage of the whole of this complicated bill. Here he was, expressing considerable sympathy for senior citizens who would need their refunds in order to meet the pressures of increased living costs. Oh, it was a grand scene. I do not know whether the minister watched the Oscar presentations and was trying to emulate them. Perhaps he felt a twinge of regret because he was not able to participate and show how good an actor he can be at times.
I would have sent my Indian princess.

I hope that with the passage of this bill, I trust tonight, the other place will be able to attend to it with appropriate consideration. Although the minister stated the other day he felt he had substantially complied with the undertakings given to the Senate by the former minister of finance at the time of the indecently hasty passage of Bill C-259 by the other place, I am now told by my connections and those working there that they do not quite feel that way toward the bill. They feel there are some major gaps. It may be these are in the remaining provisions which we will see at some time.
I do not know what the minister intends to do with regard to the corporate tax cuts to manufacturing and processing industries. Incidentally, I want to reiterate something which has escaped the attention of almost all members of this House. All corporations, from the two-man trucking outfit with "Ltd." or "Inc." behind its name to the major corporations in this country engaged in manufacturing and processing, will be faced with a tax increase of up to 7 per cent as of January 1, 1973. This exists on a parallel scale with the potential increase in taxation for individuals because last year the minister said it was impossible to do anything with regard to tax cuts for individuals. He said it would lead the country into bankruptcy. This was totally wrong. Of course, Saul was converted on the road to Damascus.
The government got around the tax cut for the individual, but it has not done anything with regard to the restoration of the 7 per cent tax cut given by Mr. Benson on October 15, 1971, and which was applicable for the last

April 12, 1973
Income Tax Act
half of 1971 and all of 1972. The grocer, farm equipment distributor, automobile garage, paint contractor, plumber and all others who are incorporated will have a tax increase for 1973 of up to 7 per cent. It is true there is a cutback under the statute from 50 per cent to 49 per cent, and from 25 per cent to 24 per cent, but the restoration of the 7 per cent and the combination works out to about 5.8 per cent. It is strange that no one has mentioned this. The press has said very little about it; the financial writers said very little about it until ten days ago.
I want to reiterate that what is left for the House to consider in so far as individuals are concerned are the goodies of the 1973 budget. There are also leftovers of the corporate tax reduction provisions and incentives of 1972, and there may be some administrative changes. We will have to wait and see. If this tax bill is put through tonight, I invite the minister to let us see the ways and means motion for implementation of the balance of the budgetary provisions. This includes not only income tax but the Customs tariff. There have been some unilateral cuts in the Customs tariff. Attention was directed to these at the time of the budget debate. While the Customs tariff bill proposed by the minister will go through fairly expeditiously, he had better reconcile himself to the fact that the next one will get a great deal more scrutiny and will receive a great deal more criticism.
Some industries have had their guts ripped by the minister's proposals. This is something we should be worried about. I do not know what motivated the government to make these proposals on a unilateral basis when we were just starting on the next round of multilateral trade negotiations. I do not know what kind of gesture it was for Canada to just toss away a great number of its negotiating points. The minister shakes his head. Let him talk to the people in the industries affected. He will get a different reaction.
Some of my colleagues want to speak about the changes that have been made with regard to capital gains as they apply to the family farm owned by the individual taxpayer. The minister confirmed this afternoon that the amendment that was brought in in addition to the provisions to exempt farmlands of a deemed realization on death, if passage was to a child or a descendant of a child there could be an inter vivos sale to a member of the family within that limitation. However, there has been no provision for a roll-over by the taxpayer in selling an orchard property and buying a corn growing property or something suited to a change in his farming practice. Whether the farm is owned by an individual or not has not been included in the legislation. This will prove to be quite a disappointment to the whole of the farming community in Canada.
My colleagues will be making more eloquent pleas with regard to the corporate family farm. I will leave the details to them. The minister has made other changes with regard to the smoother working of Bill C-259, or the Income Tax Act of 1971 and the application rules, particularly clause 78 where he has given a further two years' grace in the foreign, affiliated property inclusion, the FAPI rules, because a great many Canadian corporations will face tremendous administrative problems or potential

problems this year. Personally, I hope the minister will scrap the whole idea that gave rise to FAPI.
A Canadian company might have a holding of 2 per cent or 5 per cent in a foreign company, yet the Canadian government was insisting that this so-called foreign affiliate file financial returns in Canada. I wonder at the effrontery of Canadian tax authorities in trying to impose that regulation. If such legislation existed in the United Kingdom or in the United States we would be screaming that a foreign government was trying to make Canadian companies comply with the law in the United States or Britain, even though all we held was an ownership of shares or a joint ownership of interest in a third company.
All I can suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and to his colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) is that some of these foreign companies will not-so-politely thumb their noses, and there is nothing the Canadian government can do about it. I think it is a can of worms of the worst kind.
How does that grab you, John?

I would hope that since the minister has already taken 18 months to come up with the idea that he cannot work out the rules, he will decide to scrap the whole blessed thing, because to me it is totally wrong. I hope I have said enough with regard to this matter and, hopefully, we can get the bill through third reading tonight.

We have had a thorough discussion of this bill, Mr. Speaker, so I intend to take only two or three minutes. We are supporting the bill, as I said earlier, because it deals with individuals, giving individual people a tax break and more exemptions in terms of medical expenses, student allowances, and so on. I should like to thank the minister publicly for amending the bill in the two places he did, concerning capital gains for farmers and the amendment by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I think this is proof positive that parliament is starting to work and that we can make parliament work if we all get down to it as MPs and make up our minds to do something that is good and beneficial for individual Canadians.
The elimination of capital gains tax on farms will go a long way to preserving family farms not just in western Canada but right across the country. I think the minister should be complimented on accepting a very good NDP idea which has been promoted for years-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Put your rubber boots on.

-in this House by, among others, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave). Hon. members will also recall the amendment moved in this House last year by the then hon. member for Regina East, Mr. John Burton.

What happened to him?
April 12, 1973

What happened to him? After the Gallup poll, I am sure he will be back, with the Conservative party taking a thumping as they did in the last Gallup poll. I should like to assure hon. members on my right that he will be back and that many other New Democrats will be back from the Prairies, British Columbia and Ontario.
With that, I would like to say we support the bill. It deals with individuals. It is interesting to look at the last seven or eight budgets of the government. The first seven gave all kinds of tax exemptions and benefits to corporations. If we add them all up, we find that the first seven budgets reduced taxes to corporations by half a billion dollars and that taxes to individuals went up by $1.5 billion. In the last budget the government ignored corporations and concentrated instead on doing things for the average citizen. This is another example of making parliament work, setting an example that our party likes. I can assure the minister that if he wants to bring in more tax reform measures to block some of the loopholes for the wealthy, tax reforms to tax the resource industries more heavily, he can count on our party to help him make parliament work and pass that legislation as well, because I believe these are things that must be done in order to help the average Canadian citizen, in order to get this country really moving again.
The Conservatives would like hand-outs for the big boys, but this does not really get the economy rolling. If we want to get moving and increase employment, we must help the average citizen, the average worker, farmer and small businessman. That is the way to get this country on its feet and that is the way to create jobs. If the minister is interested in doing that, we will help him make parliament work and change this country in a really profound and significant way.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: That is the Liberal way.
Who needs Burton when you've got Nystrom?

Mr. Speaker, I could not let this opportunity pass without mentioning a few things. The main change has been in the family farm tax situation and the roll-over during the lifetime of parent and son. But nothing has been settled about the partnership family farm and nothing has been settled about the corporate family farm. Capitalization of these farms is becoming fairly large, at $100,000 even for smaller ones. Their owners are looking at the limited liability clause that covers corporations. These farms account for a significant part of our agricultural basic production.
We are now becoming interested again in food production. At long last the food glut seems to be ending and we are looking for ways and means of increasing the food supply. The rural population has dropped to a point at which it is probably getting impossible to continue to produce food in a great amounts as in the past, and unless the corporate family farm is dealt with, it will suffer the same liability that occurred prior to the repentance of the government in so far as the family farm was concerned. I think this is especially important because these farms tend to be the most productive in agriculture.
There may be one more important item, one which has been brought to my attention by many farmers who have large amounts of capital invested in their farm machines.
Income Tax Act
This is the loss of straight line depreciation, so-called, which was used by the farmers to keep their machinery a1 a high level of efficiency. It probably has contributed to the fact that food prices remain low, because productivity was extremely high.
Mechanization on the farm carries through into the service end and straight through into farm machinery manufacturing. This is extremely important, because whereas the capital gains tax will occur only occasionally, fortunately, in a family where there is a death or where there is a passing on from one generation to the next by selling, this straight line depreciation occurs every year, and it is the means by which much of the agricultural industry is able to keep at a high level of efficiency. The loss of this straight line depreciation has been severely felt by all.
Now I should like to comment on the capital gains tax as applied to small businesses as well as farms. It is too bad the government cannot see fit to make a start in looking at this area. I mention this in particular because it is an extremely onerous burden on taxpayers in a province to face both an estate tax and a capital gains tax. I have come to the conclusion that one can live with a capital gains tax or with an estate tax, but it is pretty difficult to live with both and still have a viable small business. I do not think it bothers large corporations, but it is a very serious thing for small business. We have suddenly discovered in this House, and so has even the NDP, that small business is important. Under the foreign takeover bill we are studying ways and means to permit Canadians to own more of their own country, and in this area we often start with the very large corporations. If Canadians are to own their own country, one place where we can make a significant effort is at the small business and small corporation level.
I suggest it is most important that the federal government and the provinces work together on this and cooperate to make sure that an estate tax and capital gains tax together do not bring about the dissolution of small businesses that have to be sold out piece by piece to pay those taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments of the time of the House to register some reservations regarding the measure before us. First of all, I should like to talk for a moment about the 1972 tax return. Much money has been spent on advertising this so-called very simple form which Fred Davis says is easier than you think, but strangely enough never in the history of Canada during the last 100 years have so many people been so frustrated over a new tax policy. Never have so many people had to seek professional help in order to figure out the complex, eight-page document that is presently in the hands of every taxpayer in Canada.
I am reminded of the opposition to the medicare bill which was before the House some years ago. The doctors opposed it vehemently, saying that it was one of the things that would ruin this country. Yet in fact that very legislation guaranteed the medical profession of this country a salary beyond anything they had ever experienced before,

April 12, 1973
Income Tax Act
for the rest of their lives. This tax measure has done the same thing for the accounting profession; this can be verified simply by talking to accountants. As a result of this bill and others that we have dealt with, the government have guaranteed the accounting profession of this country a pension payable every April 30 from now on.
I am a little concerned about what one of the previous speakers said. He said he was very happy that the problem of capital gains tax on farms had been resolved. I do not think it has been fully resolved at all. This afternoon in the House the minister got to his feet and clearly indicated that so far as the family farm was concerned, he had made concessions to the one-owner farms. However, he did not deal clearly enough with the position of corporate or partnership farms.
I think the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) expressed his concern about the need for clarification in regard to what would happen in a situation where a father and son or three brothers in a partnership owned a farm and one of them died. That situation has not been clarified. Neither do I understand the statement made by an NDP member a moment ago to the effect that that party was delighted at the clarification of the minister. As I say, I do not think the position has been clarified at all, and it needs to be clarified later.
The position of the family farm vis-a-vis capital gains is also not clear to me or to a number of farmers across the country. Neither is it clear in the minds of revenue officials. It is alarming to find so many people telephoning the revenue department in their respective areas and finding officials, who are supposed to be knowledgeable in the law, uptight, close-mouthed, refusing to give information. The only information people can get from the revenue offices is that they must wait a while because there will be a ruling coming from Ottawa.
One other matter that needs clarification was raised in the House previously and has been the subject of much discussion. I refer to the sale of milk quotas in the dairy industry. If a milk quota is sold, is it regarded as goodwill as in the case of a conventional business? I think the minister should be responsible to see that regulations governing the sale of quotas are spelled out clearly.
As a result of the new tax measures, property such as farms, cottages and rental property which is owned by taxpayers is now being arbitrarily assessed for purposes of capital gain at some time in the future. Does the minister not feel that the assessments obtained by the revenue officials should become the property of the taxpayer himself? I understand that when revenue officials assess a piece of property, whether it be a farm, cottage or rental property, attempts are made to secure information for the file of the taxpayer so as to determine the amount of the assessment. It is my understanding that this assessment is then fed into a computer and eventually will be used against the taxpayer. I do not think we need to use this kind of, if you like, gestapo tactic in Canada in order to obtain information on taxpayers which is fed into computers and used ultimately against the taxpayer.
The government today has made inroads into the office of every business in this country. It is a shame the government is not satisfied with the taxes that are paid by business enterprises and leave it at that. I owned a small

business a few years ago and required, on average, about one and a half people in the office just to look after the demands of government, such as figuring out deductions for medicare, unemployment insurance and everything else. It is time the government relieved some of the pressure it is putting on the business community of Canada.
Although I am quite prepared to go along with the concessions the minister has made up to this point, I hope that by the time the next budget rolls around he will have seriously considered the criticism which members of the opposition, particularly those of the Conservative party, have made and that he will come up with some new proposals in 1973.

subtopic: FISHERIES-STORM DAMAGE IN NEWFOUNDLAND LAST NOVEMBER-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT AND COMPENSATION TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not realize that everybody was so efficient. It is so long since I requested the debate at this time on a question I asked in the House of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), seeking a more substantial reply, that the answer is now probably obsolete.
The question I asked on November 19 in relation to storm damage in Newfoundland last fall has been answered, not only by the minister before the committee but in the House after follow-up questions and by departmental officials in the committee. I must say those answers were not much help in any event. My question related to the involvement of the federal government in respect of storm damage, which occurred last fall in western Newfoundland, to fishing gear, stores, longliners and other fishing vessels, some of which were completely destroyed. In answer to my question in the House, to my surprise the minister indicated that so far as the federal government was concerned, his responsibility only arose when vessel insurance was concerned and it was left to the provinces to compensate for losses to fishermen, regardless of the extent.
Even though we have to accept the cold fish attitude of the minister, which is becoming his trademark as well as that of other officials, fishermen were led to believe that compensation would be considered, on a co-operative basis, by the two levels of government. I suppose we must accept the decision of the federal government that unless the damage was on the basis of a national emergency, the federal government has no responsibility.
I refer to the matter again tonight as there is still an area of concern in which the minister can help, and that is in relation to fishermen who did not have vessel insurance because they could not afford it. I refer to fishermen whose longliners were damaged by the storm last fall and still remain unrepaired.
As the fishing season approaches, we find there are no funds available to assist these fishermen in putting their boats back into the water. In addition to this, there is a perennial problem which the fishermen face. They are willing to compete with foreign draggers, but cannot find the means to purchase these vessels because of the restrictions under the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act and under the Newfoundland fisheries loan board because of the down payment required. Under the loan board, a fisherman or a group of fishermen who want to invest in a longliner, the cost of which runs to $50,000 or more, cannot find the required 10 per cent down payment even though they have the initiative and the knowledge to compete with others and are allowed to compete without restriction.
The government should act out of humane consideration for and faith in Newfoundland fishermen and provide for a review of the restrictions imposed on these fishermen. The government should provide incentives and the opportunity for these fishermen to provide not only for themselves but for neighbouring fishermen. I ask the minister to consider this aspect of the industry. I am not one who criticizes unnecessarily, but I submit this idea which I know the minister will consider, in view of his

April 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
interest, of providing funds necessary to all Newfoundland fishermen to contribute to the Canadian economy, not only to the benefit of Canada but to their own livelihood. I ask that consideration be given to this matter and that the minister provide answers to my submission.

subtopic: FISHERIES-STORM DAMAGE IN NEWFOUNDLAND LAST NOVEMBER-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT AND COMPENSATION TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to the loss of fishing gear in Newfoundland. He refers to the fact, also, that the federal government has refused, so far at least, to compensate fishermen for loss of gear. He refers to me personally as being a cold fish minister. The people of Canada, through the government of Canada, have set up and administered the only insurance program which exists to cover losses of fishermen. There is no such program at the provincial level. The program which does exist relates to commercial fishing vessels and all gear fixed to those vessels. It is a form of insurance available at very low rates. It has been extended at exceptionally low rates to insure fishermen especially in the province of Newfoundland.
There was also an attempt two years ago to include as insurable gear miscellaneous gear, but the fishermen did not see fit to pay the very modest premiums charged for this. Indeed, very few of them signed in the initial stages. That program, therefore, was abandoned because there was no, or little income available to it. It could not work as an insurance plan. It is still a challenge. It is an opportunity for the province because it relates to small gear for small people in outlying places. This is the kind of program which a province could well administer.
I do not know what the Department of Fisheries really does at the provincial level. If it cannot handle this kind of thing, I do not understand how it can handle any larger program. We have joined with the province in many surveys, including surveys of gear damage. The province knows what the damage is. It has also known for a long time that this relatively small program is a logical one for the province to carry out, and it has failed to do its job in this connection.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF RADIO PRODUCTION AT DON MILLS PLANT OF PHILCO-FORD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF RADIO PRODUCTION AT DON MILLS PLANT OF PHILCO-FORD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I managed to get two words across a while ago. They were simply "I wonder". I was beginning to wonder then whether there would be somebody here from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am glad to see that the parliamentary secretary is here.
My question tonight is an extension of the question I asked last Friday morning at a time when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) was not in the House. It had to do with the partial shut-down of a plant in Don Mills, Ontario, owned by Philco-Ford of Canada. It appears that the plant intends to shut down one part of its operation concerned with the production of car radios for sale and resale to the Ford Motor Company of Canada. It turns out, from all the evidence, that this is indeed a very efficient part of this plant, so it could not be for reasons of efficiency that they are closing it down or for reasons of labour costs. We know the average wage rate in that section of the plant is some $2.90 an hour and

that, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, in the Toronto region is no fortune.
However, some excuse is made for shutting down this part of the plant and throwing out about 100 employees on the ground that they are simply assembly-line workers, not many of whom are skilled and, as it says in the article, most of whom are women. I do not particularly like that aspect, but there you have it. I suppose women, in the world of industry, are more expendable.
The reasons for shutting down that part of the plant, as given by the managers and owners of the plant, are for the sake of economy. According to the trade union representatives of the workers in that plant, the total labour cost for the car radios produced in the plant, per radio, is $3. The total cost of labour and materials is $13. The radios themselves sell for $90. It is evident that $3 is a very small part of $90. It appears that the plant operates very well and very economically. But Philco-Ford is going to move this operation to a larger operation it is setting up in Brazil. They intend to produce, apparently, all their radios for all their world sales in Brazil.
So there we have it, a multinational corporation, for reasons of its own-its views on rationalization and economy-deciding to wipe out the jobs of about 100 Canadian workers. Surely this decision was not made with the interest of these workers in mind, and certainly not with the interest of the Canadian economy in mind.
My question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce at the time was simply whether anything could be done under the terms of the auto pact to intervene in this matter and somehow persuade this company not to "rationalize" its operations-I put the word "rationalize" in quotation marks-to the detriment of the workers of Don Mills and to the detriment of Canada. The components for these radios made at Don Mills come from Taiwan. They are not made in Canada. They are brought in duty-free under some aspect of the auto pact.
What we could ask, further, is whether the car radios which will be made in Brazil will be brought in duty-free. We might ask, even further, just how many components for cars to be produced in Canada will be brought in from outside the country duty-free. I have asked these questions in the hope that the minister can say there is something that can be done under the auto pact to prevent this kind of thing. However, I must say I am in despair of getting that kind of answer. I am too sure, unfortunately, that the minister, with regard to this particular pact, is impotent. I do not really think he can do anything.
I wish that in answer to my question he would say it would be possible for him to intervene to preserve these jobs for the Canadian workers. At any rate, I wait with some expectation and perhaps some faint hope that if I cannot get that kind of answer, we can get from this government some day in the future some backbone, some mettle and some spirit to protect the jobs of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister oi Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF RADIO PRODUCTION AT DON MILLS PLANT OF PHILCO-FORD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was reasonable in his question when he asked whether there was something the minister could do under the auto pact. Unfortunately, as the hon. member knows, under the auto pact the auto companies are required,
April 12, 1973

under contract, to keep a fair level of production in Canada in respect of the production of vehicles in ratio to the markets in Canada and the Canadian contracts with CDA. When the companies have complied with that provision, there is no legal authority under which the government could oblige Philco-Ford or the Ford Company of Canada to do anything in respect of its components. We sympathize, of course, with the social dislocation which some people might feel but, unfortunately, in our type of economy, unless there is a legal requirement there is nothing we can do.
I would like to say also that Philco-Ford of Canada is also engaged in the manufacture of stereo and television sets at the Don Mills plant. The company has enjoyed substantial market success over the last five years and the average level of hourly employees at the plant increased from 330 in 1967 to 580 in 1972.
The transfer of car radio production to Brazil will affect 122 workers. The company will retain 47 of these workers in the production of other products at the Don Mills plant, and it is expected that the balance of 75 workers could be laid off in July, 1973. However, the company is hopeful that the market demand for its stereo and television products will enable it to retain a number of the employees scheduled for lay-off in July. So we hope that the markets in the other products will justify keeping the other employees.
I would like to say that it is very unfortunate that multinational corporations do this, but we must admit that in other circumstances we have benefited from such shifts in production. For example, there has been a lot of criticism in the United States that under the auto pact, production has been shifted by these corporations from the United States to Canada. So while sometimes, in this world of international economics we have to give and take, this is one of the "gives", but sometimes we have the "takes".
I am sorry that this has to happen, but the company cites lower production costs as the reason for the transfer. That is the reason the company gave to the department. Also, they have transferred production from the United States. It seems they want to develop some kind of captive production in what is probably the only plant of its kind in the world; so they shifted that type of production from other countries also. We know they shifted it from the United States to Brazil. We are sorry this has happened and we hope the employees will be able to stay on.

We cannot allow points of order at this time. The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) has the floor.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-EXPIRATION OF FISHERIES BENEFITS-POSSIBLE EQUATING OF BENEFIT PERIOD WITH QUALIFYING PERIOD-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am disappointed that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is not here to answer my question. He is the minister in charge of the department which now has jurisdiction over unemployment insurance for everybody in Canada, I presume. I want to raise a question which is a very difficult one to raise during the regular question period, because it is a somewhat complicated matter and I think most members of the House, and indeed the general public, are not aware of the issue.
If I were to put the issue in the form of a general question, it would be to ask the government and the Minister of the Environment or his representative today, who obviously wants to go to bat for him, what the government has against the fishermen of this country. I will say right now that if I ever become a member of a governing party which will not be able to do more for the fishermen of Canada than the present government, I will not support that government. I make that commitment to the fishermen of this country. I will not support a government that allows discrimination, the worst form of discrimination that I have witnessed in the last number of years, and I will not be satisfied with the minister reading 1,500 words of a prepared text.
I want a legitimate answer and I promise I will pursue this matter as long as I am a Member of Parliament until it is duly rectified by this government or a succeeding government. We have a system of unemployment insurance for fishermen which is at least 100 years old in concept. This year, for example, in our province there will be about $70 million and last year $73 million went into the province in the form of unemployment insurance as a whole. That was the total cost to the federal treasury, minus whatever was paid by the contributors.
In order to rectify the injustice now being perpetrated on the fishermen, it might cost the government another $1 million or $1,200,000 or a little bit more. For two years the minister has indicated before the committee and before the House that they are working on a plan for the fishermen. There are three ways to present a full-blown plan that would improve the lot of the fishermen. At the moment a man working in any capacity in Canada, in the

Adjournment Debate
automotive factories or as a carpenter or labourer, who has eight weeks' stamps and is in a very high unemployment area like the Maritimes, can receive approximately one year of benefits. In other words, he can work for two months and get approximately one year's benefits. Some people argue that this is excessive. A fishermen with eight weeks' stamps, the man who catches the fish to keep the fish plants going, gets 61 weeks' benefits; in other words, only five-sixths of the number of stamps. A labourer or carpenter or anyone else gets six times as many benefits as he has stamps. If you add that up, the stamp that any regular worker receives is approximately seven times as good as the stamp the fisherman receives.
The minister will say that the fisherman is an independent worker and does not deserve any benefits at all. Coupled with the foregoing, however, he is not able to draw benefit until the middle of December and it continues, if he has enough stamps-he must have approximately 30 weeks' credit in order to draw for the full off-season- until the middle of May. Unless he is among the top 10 per cent of fishermen in Canada, he is forced to go on welfare from approximately March until the fishing season starts in earnest, which is approximately June.
On top of that, the fisherman has to average the last 20 weeks' benefits in order to come up with the rate of return that he would get from his stamps if he is really industrious and wants to work through October and November. Instead of being credited for the determination to continue, he gets a lower stamp because his average is down. If he quits at the beginning of September having had eight or ten weeks of very good fishing, he is all right; but if he continues into the stormy fall of the year he is penalized.
These are three or four ways in which the government could amend the present program for the fishermen in order to give them some justice. The government has concluded that the fishermen in Canada are not a very potent force. It is not compatible with the government's political aspirations in the larger urban centres to treat these people with any respect, and consequently they are being trampled upon. That is the reason the government is refusing to move. The minister is aware of the injustice, because I have already moved a motion and have talked to him in committee, and also to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. But they will not budge. I
I am going to carry this cause even across the Canadian nation until the people of Canada see that the fishermen are not being given a square deal. I want the minister to give us some assurance that at least the government will move toward making the fisherman's stamp at least partly equal to the stamp given to the regular Canadian worker. I ask that the fisherman be given as many benefit weeks as the number of stamps he has. For most, that would mean four or five weeks' benefits to tide them over until the fishing season starts. I submit that would cost the treasury almost nothing and would give our fishermen at
least part of a square deal-a square deal that they are not now getting.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-EXPIRATION OF FISHERIES BENEFITS-POSSIBLE EQUATING OF BENEFIT PERIOD WITH QUALIFYING PERIOD-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Gander-Twiliingate (Mr. Lundrigan) made several criticisms of our present unemployment insurance scheme as it applies to the fisheries in Canada. One, at least, I think is valid, the requirement that under present law the fisherman can only record his last 20 weeks of fishing in order to determine his benefits. A fisherman, naturally, would want to record for benefit purposes his best weeks and, therefore, under the present system he is tempted to stop fishing when his catch begins to taper off. Under the new amendments proposed and tabled, actually they have received first reading in the House, that problem will be overcome. So I would urge the hon. member to support the legislation in order to overcome the 20-week problem which he mentioned.
The main purport of the hon. member's remarks was that the fisherman is being discriminated against. The fisherman has a difficult time of it, but he is the only category of self-employed person in Canada who is receiving the benefit of unemployment insurance. For example, farmers do not. Farmers, unlike self-employed fishermen, are not eligible for unemployment insurance.
The hon. member concluded that most factory workers can work for eight or ten weeks, or some short period, and enjoy as much as one year of benefits. That, indeed, would be an exceptional case; perhaps 1 or 2 per cent of all factory workers are ever in the position of working as little as eight weeks and then drawing one year of benefits. On the other hand, fishermen every year draw a benefit. Many of the better fishermen draw benefits every year from December 1 to March 15 as a regular practice. As a broad generalization, fishermen pay about $1 into the scheme and get $10 out. They pay, in total in this country, about $2 in each year and get $20 million out. So the fisherman gets a pretty good deal under unemployment insurance.
I am not saying that the unemployment insurance scheme is tailored to his particular circumstances. It is not. It is a scheme which was developed basically for factory workers. We need a better scheme that is tailored to the needs of fishermen. However, the present scheme is much enriched over the one of a couple of years ago. I remind the hon. member that it was the Liberal government that brought in the scheme. The Conservatives were in power for nearly half a dozen years and did nothing about it. It has been enriched several times since. We will, in one year or two when the present unemployment insurance scheme shakes down and when it is working well, develop an alternative scheme that will apply to fishermen. We will develop a scheme that the fishermen will like better. I hope the hon. member will support us in that scheme.
